member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Dto.GenesysRoutingUpdateDto
member.summary:
Where the conversation is now — the queue it sits in and the agent it is connected to. Sent on a queue change, when an agent connects, and on every transfer; always the same conversation, the same interaction and the same ticket.
It records the conversation's current routing and nothing about the ticket: no department, owner or status moves because Genesys transferred a call. The first agent who handled the interaction stays recorded as its handler. When an agent connects to a conversation whose human work is still WaitingForAgent, that is the human taking it, and the work is marked assigned to them exactly as handoff.assignedAgentId would.
member.param: The Genesys queue the conversation is now in.
That queue's display name.

The Genesys User ID of the agent now connected (answered / accepted — never one that is merely ringing or assigned). Resolved to the mapped Ticketing user and recorded as a handler of the interaction, so every agent a transfer passes through is kept.
That agent's display name. Display only — never an identity key.
When that agent connected, as Genesys reports it (the participant's connected time). Optional; stored on the handler record when supplied.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Dto.GenesysHandoffUpdateDto
member.summary: Human-agent state for the conversation, on any channel. A callback is one possible , never the concept.
member.param: True records that the conversation needs a human agent — idempotent, as a conversation whose human work is still outstanding is answered with that same work item. Explicit false stands outstanding work down (the AI resumed, or the human is no longer needed) and requires . Null (omitted) does neither, which is what lets an update carry only without the omitted flag reading as a cancellation — the reason this is nullable rather than a plain bool.
True when Genesys is handing straight over to a named human, false when nobody is available and the work must wait.
"Callback", "ContinueChat", "ReplyInChannel" or "HumanTakeover". Omit unless Genesys actually states it — TigerCS never derives it from the channel.
Why a human is needed (a virtual agent's escalation reason, a routing note) — or, when standing work down, why the human is no longer needed. Required in that direction.

Why a human is needed, typed: "CustomerRequestedHuman", "AiConnectionLost", "AiEscalated", "RoutingDecision" or "AgentTransfer". Omit unless Genesys states it — never derived from the channel or the end reason.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.GenesysOptions
member.summary:
The Genesys integration's own settings — a plain value in the Application layer (the composition root binds configuration onto it, exactly as ReopenPolicy and OutboxDispatchPolicy do, so this project keeps depending on nothing but the Domain).
is the feature flag. False — the default — means every Genesys ingestion entry point answers "integration disabled" and writes nothing; manual/Face-to-Face ticket creation, the New Ticket wizard, and every existing flow behave exactly as they did before this phase. Nothing in the normal ticketing path reads this flag, which is what makes that guarantee structural rather than a promise.
No Genesys credential or endpoint lives here. Ticketing exposes inbound endpoints only. Genesys Cloud authenticates with OAuth 2.0 client credentials to TigerGroupWeb, which forwards to these endpoints as an authenticated TigerCS service account through the system's existing JWT authentication. TigerCS never calls Genesys' own API, so none of it (base URL, OAuth client) is configured here.

member.summary: The code of the department that acts as the safe classification queue (Genesys:ClassificationDepartmentCode, e.g. the department whose staff triage Unclassified tickets). Used only when configuration cannot place a Genesys ticket: no department, queue mapping or valid request type named one, or a supplied request type is unusable (unmapped intent, retired department, no published workflow). The ticket is then created Unclassified in this department for a person to classify, rather than being refused (and the customer's request lost) or routed on a guess. Resolved by code against the Departments table — never an id in code. Unset (the default) keeps the previous behaviour: an unroutable inquiry or an unusable request type is refused with 422 and nothing is created.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.ChatbotInactivityCloseAppService
member.summary:
Two rules, never both on one ticket.
Website/Chatbot (current): a ticket whose Genesys chat conversation is tracked () closes when the customer has done nothing for more than (default 10 minutes) since their last interaction — never since ticket creation. Each customer message restarts it. Reason: .
Bot-prompt (original): for everything that rule does not track (voice, Call Center, rows from before it), the chatbot waited more than (5) for an answer. Unchanged.
Call Center tickets (originating or current department) and human-managed tickets (owner, handler, open handoff) are never closed by the first rule; a candidate found to be out of scope simply stops being tracked. A ticket already closed — e.g. by document delivery — is never touched again.
Closes a ticket whose chatbot has been waiting on the customer for longer than the configured time (, default 5 minutes). Driven by a recurring server-side job — never by a client — reading TicketInteractions.AwaitingCustomerReplySinceUtc, so the timeout survives restarts and deploys.
Re-checked at fire time, in this order, before anything is written: the integration is on and a timeout is configured; the interaction still carries a timer that is strictly older than the timeout (a customer reply clears it; a repeated webhook never moved it); the conversation has not ended; no human follow-up is open (requested handoff, bot connection failure — both raise a ); no person owns the ticket (a human assignment); the ticket is still open for work. Any exclusion cancels the timer so it stops being a candidate, and closes nothing.
Race with a customer reply. The timer column is a concurrency token. The interaction is loaded, checked, and its timer cleared in the same SaveChanges as the ticket closure; if a reply cleared the timer in between, that write affects zero rows and the whole closure rolls back (). The reply wins.
Idempotent. The interaction's InactivityClosedAtUtc is write-once and the Outbox lifecycle event has its own idempotency key, so a repeated run, an overlapping run or a Hangfire retry closes once and notifies once.
The closure goes through : the lifecycle's Resolved→Closed transitions, with outcome Cancelled — never "Resolved" — and the audit reason below.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.GenesysAgentContextAppService
member.summary:
The Genesys agent action entry point: a Genesys agent's session (the Ticketing screen opened from Genesys) identifies itself, and Ticketing answers with exactly which Ticketing user that agent is — and, when the agent is working a conversation, records that user as the one who handled the conversation's interaction.
Strict, because this represents an agent. Unlike the inquiry and update events (which a queue or system may send before any agent exists), this request is an agent acting, so the Genesys User ID is required, and an unmapped or deactivated agent is refused with a distinct outcome rather than being let through anonymously.
Ownership is resolved here, on the server, from the Genesys User ID alone. The request carries no Ticketing user id and none would be honoured: HandledByUserId is whatever the mapping resolves to, never what a client claims.
Records who handled the interaction — nothing else. The ticket's assignee, department, queue, status and workflow are untouched: "handled the conversation" and "owns the ticket" are different facts, and only the first is this service's to write.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.GenesysAgentHandlingHistory
member.summary:
The ticket's record of which Genesys agents actually handled the customer, kept in the existing typed workflow event history (no table of its own).
Handling is not escalation. A Genesys call transfer says an agent passed the conversation on, not that they failed to resolve it, so these events carry no transfer reason: they are never escalations and never count as ticket transfers. Only an explicit TigerCS transfer or reassignment, with a reason chosen by a person, records that.
A timeline, not the source of truth for who handled the interaction. The per-agent record of who handled a Genesys interaction - and so who may see the ticket - is TicketInteractionHandlers, owned by the CS Agent visibility work. These events are the ORDERED story shown on the ticket: who answered first (also HandledByUserId, apply-if-absent), then each step "agent X passed the call to agent Y", including agents with no TigerCS user (kept verbatim in the note). Nothing here grants or removes visibility, nothing reads these events to decide access, and nothing here writes a handler row. Nothing changes ticket ownership either - who handled the call and who owns the ticket stay different facts.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.GenesysAgentHandoffAppService
member.summary:
The inbound half of pending human work: Genesys reporting that an interaction needs a human agent, and later that one has taken it.
This is not "a callback request". Genesys carries phone, website chat, chatbot, WhatsApp, social media and more. On every one of them the same thing happens — routing or a virtual agent decides a human is needed — and the business rule is identical: do not lose the inquiry, and make it visible to agents. Only the continuation differs, and a callback is one of those modes rather than the concept.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.GenesysConversationEndAppService
member.summary:
Genesys integration phase 1 — finalizing a conversation and preserving its transcript.
Ending a conversation never closes a ticket. This is the phase's load-bearing business rule and the reason this service touches the aggregate only to read it: the chat ends, the interaction is marked ended, and the ticket carries on under the existing TigerCS lifecycle — a customer who asked for an NOC has an open workflow long after the chat window closed. No status, SLA, resolution or escalation state is written here.
Every disconnection is an ending. The customer closing the browser, losing signal, the agent ending the interaction, or Genesys terminating it are all the same call: whatever end time and reason are supplied are recorded, and the transcript available up to that moment is stored. A conversation that ended abruptly still leaves a complete record of what was said.
Idempotent, without losing anything. is write-once, so a redelivered end answers and never moves the recorded end time or reason. Its transcript is still read, though, and any message not already stored is appended — deduplicated on Genesys' own message id where one is supplied, and otherwise on sender+timestamp+body. That is what makes "the COMPLETE transcript is persisted" true rather than "whatever the first delivery happened to carry": a chat stored from a truncated first delivery is completed by the retry instead of staying permanently short. The transcript is validated in full before anything is written, so a malformed message can never leave a half-stored conversation.
Ending a conversation is not a request for a human. The AI finishing, the customer leaving, a closed browser tab and a dropped connection all end a conversation, and none of them says a person is needed — so by default no handoff is raised here. Human work exists only when Genesys signals it explicitly (handoff.required = true). The previous "safety net" that raised an handoff for any AI conversation ended without a human is kept behind Genesys:AutoRaiseHandoffOnConversationEnd (default off) as a rollback lever; see for its conditions.

Stores messages of a conversation that is still going on (or has just ended) — the incremental half of the transcript, so a human who takes the interaction can read what the customer and the AI already said before replying.
Additive and idempotent. Messages are only ever appended, in delivered order, and never edited or removed. A message is recognised as already stored by Genesys' messageId when it has one, and otherwise by sender + timestamp + body; an id-bearing message also matches a stored row that had no id (the same line first sent without one), so the final transcript on conversation end reconciles with the incremental deliveries instead of duplicating them. A whole transcript is validated before anything is written.
Nothing about the ticket moves: the interaction is not ended, no handoff is raised, status is untouched. Only a genuinely human line can record First Response (same rule as the end event); bot lines never can.
Adds every message not already stored, in delivered order, continuing the stored sequence.

Satisfies the First Response SLA from the transcript, when the conversation contains a genuinely human reply and the ticket does not already carry one.
The measured moment is the human's FIRST message, ordered by the transcript's own Sequence — not the end of the conversation and not now. What the SLA measures is when the customer first heard from a person, and that is the timestamp on that line.
lines are deliberately invisible here, as are and lines. An AI reply is not a first human response: FR-SLA-05/ISSUE-019 exist because a machine answering in seconds would satisfy every target automatically and make the KPI meaningless — which is also why accepting a handoff does not record it either (confirmed decision 10). Only a person speaking to the customer does.
Write-once is 's own guarantee and 's: a redelivered transcript re-reads the same first human line and changes nothing.

Raises pending human work when an AI conversation has ended and nobody human ever took it — the safety net behind "an AI disconnect must never orphan the ticket".
All four conditions must hold, and each rules out a case where raising work would be wrong:
The transcript carries activity. Without it this was not an AI conversation at all, and an ordinary call ending is not pending human work.
No human ever handled it — no line and no resolved HandledByUserId. A conversation a person already took needs no handoff; it had one.
No outstanding handoff exists. This is what makes the safety net invisible when Genesys did its job and sent Handoff.Required = true, and what stops a redelivered end event raising a second work item.
The ticket is not Closed. Closed-ticket immutability is a standing rule in this solution, and pending human work on a closed case is work nobody should be asked to do.
The department is the ticket's CURRENT one, exactly as GenesysAgentHandoffAppService.RequestAsync reads it: work follows a transferred ticket. And the requested-at moment is the conversation's end, not "now" — the customer has been waiting since the AI dropped them, and the Human Wait metric must measure from there.
A lost race against a concurrent handoff request surfaces at SaveChangesAsync as the filtered unique index rejecting the second open row. The caller treats that as "already requested", which it is — see EndAsync's handling.

Whether this message is already in the stored transcript.
Genesys' own message id decides it whenever one is supplied — that is what messageId is for. Without one there is no identifier to trust, so the fallback compares the facts that together identify a line of conversation: same sender, same instant, same body. Two genuinely distinct messages matching all three would be the same person saying the same thing at the same timestamp, which is a redelivery in every case that matters.

member.name: M:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.GenesysConversationEndAppService.NormalizeExternalId(System.String)
member.summary: Validates and normalizes every supplied message before a single row is written: an unknown sender or an empty body fails the whole request rather than being silently dropped or attributed to the wrong party. Order is the delivered order — never re-sorted by timestamp, because a provider clock is not guaranteed monotonic and two messages may share a timestamp.

The id as it is STORED (blank → none, trimmed, at most the column length), so a retry compares against what was kept: comparing the raw value would never match a stored id that had to be shortened, and the retry would be stored again.

The flat screen-pop projection of the full result: CRM first, then PACT, then Tasleeh — the order the New Ticket wizard presents them in. Nothing here is looked up again; it only reshapes what the sources already answered.

One entry per physical unit. Identity is the resolved unit code (CRM project code + number, or PACT's own code) — two sources agree on a unit only when their codes are equal. member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.GenesysCustomerUnitDetailsAppService
member.summary:
POST /api/genesys/customers/unit-details: the unit and project facts a chatbot/voicebot may tell a verified customer.
Authorization is decided here, against CRM, on every call. The request names a customer and (optionally) a unit, but neither is trusted. The verified phone number is looked up through — the same service the New Ticket wizard and the Genesys lookup use — and the request is served only when (1) that lookup resolves to exactly the customer the request names, and (2) the requested unit is one of that customer's own Buyer units (Sold/Contract, as CRM itself filters). A unit id alone grants nothing; a unit that exists but belongs to someone else is refused with the same answer as one that does not exist, so ids cannot be probed.
What is returned. Unit and project fields CRM's buyer lookup provides are mapped as-is. Facts that lookup does not carry (tower, bedrooms, area, parking, project address/status/description/amenities, handover dates) come from and are null whenever that source has nothing — never defaulted or derived. Unit-level and project-level handover dates are returned in separate fields. Nothing from CRM beyond the mapped fields (no internal notes, no other customer data, no contact details) is copied into the response.
Private financial data needs proof, not just ownership. The customer's actual sold price and registration cost are returned only when the request carries a verificationSessionId produced by the server's own one-time-code verification (email or SMS) for this very customer, unit and Lead, owned by the calling service account and unexpired — the same evidence document copies require. A verificationMethod a caller merely asserted is never proof, and neither is a phone number or customer id the caller typed. Without proof CRM is not even asked for the sale. With it, the sale is requested for the Lead the buyer lookup bound to this unit and discarded unless CRM echoes that same Lead, so another buyer's sale or an unrelated historical booking cannot be shown.

member.summary: The sale is private, so it needs server-recorded evidence, never an assertion. A session qualifies only when all of these hold: it is owned by the calling account, confirmed and unexpired; it carries the proof the OTP service attaches (ProofChallengeId, CrmBuyerCustomerId, CrmBuyerLeadId) — which no agent-asserted session has, whatever verificationMethod it names; the proof was bound to this CRM customer and this unit's Lead; the session's unit is this unit; and the recorded challenge itself exists, was spent by a correct code, produced this very session for this caller, and is bound to the same customer, Lead and unit. Unknown, foreign, unconfirmed, expired, asserted, other-customer, other-unit and other-Lead sessions all give the same answer (), so session ids cannot be probed. A phone number or customer id alone is never proof.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.GenesysInquiryIngestionAppService
member.summary:
Genesys integration phase 1 — the one ingestion flow every Genesys channel converges on. Phone, website chat, WhatsApp and social media do not get separate ticket-creation implementations: each arrives as the same normalized and runs the same sequence — idempotency check, channel resolution, department resolution, customer lookup, ticket creation, conversation link.
One service request, exactly one ticket. The identity of an inquiry is the pair (, ). The first accepted event for a pair creates a ticket; every retry, redelivery, or duplicate event returns that same ticket () and creates nothing. A conversation can therefore carry several distinct service requests (documents, then apartment leasing), each a separate ticket with its own lifecycle. A caller that sends no service request id keeps the original contract — the conversation is one ticket and every repeat returns it. The guarantee is not only this service's read-before-write: the pair carries a unique index on TicketInteractions, so two concurrent deliveries that both pass the read still produce one ticket — the loser's unique-constraint violation is caught below and answered with the winner's ticket.
A ringing phone never gets here. Reaching this service means a real inquiry exists: an agent picked up the call, or a digital conversation started. TigerCS is not an event receiver for call progress, so there is no Ringing/Answered vocabulary for Genesys to send — the phone flow simply begins at pickup, with the customer lookup and then this.
Nothing is re-implemented. The intake record comes from , the ticket from (ticket number, status history, SLA clock, auto-assignment, outbox, audit and the originating interaction all unchanged), and the customer identification from — the same lookup the New Ticket wizard uses. Genesys never reaches the CRM/PACT/Tasleeh gateways, or any customer database, directly.
Lookup never gates the inquiry. A customer that cannot be found, or a lookup source that is down, changes nothing: the ticket is created as an unverified customer inquiry with whatever the channel collected (name, email, tower/unit typed into the website form). A CRM/PACT outage must never make a Genesys inquiry disappear, so the lookup is wrapped and its failure recorded rather than propagated. Nor is a customer match ever auto-selected — that stays the agent's explicit act, exactly as everywhere else in this system.
The ticket is created Unclassified, on the default priority. The department (the website form's Leasing / Customer Service / Maintenance choice, or the queue mapping) is a department and nothing else: it is not a Category and not a Request Type. The ticket is created with CategoryId = null rather than filed under a placeholder, but it starts on the configured default priority (Genesys:DefaultTicketPriority, "Normal" — the Medium tier — resolved from the Priorities table, never a hard-coded id) so its SLA is measured from the first moment: the period opens at ticket creation with that priority's policy, the same clock-start rule as every other ticket. A staff member can change the priority through the existing Ticket Details flow; re-ingesting the conversation never does.
The request type, when the bot has one. A request type on the inquiry is validated and applied by right after the ticket exists: its department becomes the responsible one (through the transfer semantics, OriginatingDepartmentId untouched), the configured automatic assignment runs, and its SLA policy is applied to the running period without restarting the clock. A missing or unusable request type is not an error: the ticket is created with the default priority, stays Unclassified and is left to the existing manual classification workflow (it is not a human handoff). An explicitly invalid request type (unknown, inactive, ambiguous, cannot route) is refused with 422 before anything is written.

The one place a Genesys-supplied request type is validated and applied to a ticket — at initial ingestion and when the bot identifies it later — plus the "nobody could classify this" path into the existing human follow-up queue. Everything it does to the ticket is delegated to (transfer semantics, automatic assignment, SLA policy) and (the human follow-up queue); nothing here is a second implementation.
Idempotent and conservative. Re-sending the request type a ticket already has changes nothing; an invalid one is refused before any write. Classification never touches the first-human-response measurement.
The AI may refine its own classification — until a person has worked the ticket. A different request type replaces the current one (history kept: RequestTypeReclassified workflow event + audit entry) only while finds nothing in the way: the ticket is Open, nobody classified it by hand (no Category), no human has responded or accepted the interaction, and no approval was raised under the old type. Otherwise the change is refused with and the ticket is left exactly as it was.
A missing classification is not a human request. A ticket without a request type stays Unclassified and is picked up by the existing manual classification workflow (Classify Ticket / the Unclassified filters); no handoff row is written for it. Human work exists only when Genesys signals it explicitly through the handoff contract.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.GenesysScreenPopAppService
member.summary:
Genesys Secure Screen Pop: Genesys asks for a launch URL for one of its agents, opens it in any browser or WebView, and the agent arrives in TigerCS Web signed in as the Ticketing user their Genesys User ID maps to — with no TigerCS login cookie needed beforehand.
Issue () runs as the authenticated Genesys service account. The agent is resolved strictly — through the same agent-context flow POST /api/genesys/agent-context uses, so an unmapped or deactivated agent is refused and a conversation's interaction records its handler exactly as it does there. The landing page is chosen in priority order: the conversation's ticket, the named ticket, the customer lookup for the caller's number, the Tickets list. A 256-bit random token is minted and only its SHA-256 is stored.
Redeem () is anonymous by nature — the token is the credential. It is refused when unknown, older than one hour, or already used; the mapping is re-resolved and must still point at the same active, unlocked user. The answer is precisely the session a password login returns (, the user's own roles), so everything after sign-in is authorized exactly as for any other session: the token grants no ticket, department or page access of its own, and a target the user may not see is refused by the target page.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.GenesysTicketUpdateAppService
member.summary:
The one update contract Genesys consumes — a facade over the conversation-end and human-handoff services, not a reimplementation of either.
Why a facade. Genesys asked for three externally consumable contracts: create, look up, update. The behaviour behind "update" already existed as separate services with their own rules, idempotency and tests; splitting one integration concept across three routes made the external surface wider than the integration actually is. This composes them, so there is exactly one place Genesys sends changes and exactly one place each rule lives.
Genesys owns the conversation; TigerCS owns the ticket. The only things this accepts are conversation facts — who is handling it, when it ended, what was said, whether it needs a human. Category, request type, priority, status, owner, department, resolution and closure are absent from the contract by design: they move through their own TigerCS operations, with their own authorization and SLA consequences. Genesys cannot reach them from here at all.
Nothing in this call closes a ticket. Ending a conversation finalizes the interaction and stores the transcript; the ticket carries on under the existing lifecycle. The response echoes the ticket's unchanged status to make that visible on every call. The one automatic closure — a chatbot that waited more than the configured time for a customer reply — happens later, in ChatbotInactivityCloseAppService driven by a background job; this call only starts or cancels the persisted timer it reads.
Validated before anything is written. The conversation must resolve to an interaction on the ticket in the route — that cross-check is what stops a transcript being applied to the wrong ticket — and a malformed transcript is refused by the end service before it writes, so a bad update never leaves a half-applied conversation.

member.name: F:TigerCS.Application.Modules.GenesysIntegration.Services.GenesysTicketUpdateAppService.ClosedByAiReason
member.summary: The exact closure reason recorded when the AI finishes the conversation.

closedByAi: true — the Genesys AI finished the conversation. Closes through the lifecycle (Resolved → Closed, audit AutoCloseByAi, history, notification) with the exact reason , but ONLY while the AI still owns the conversation: no requested/pending/connected human, no person owning the ticket, not a Call Center ticket, still open. Anything else is answered with a note and changes nothing — never an error, so a retried webhook stays safe. An already-closed ticket (by a person, document delivery, inactivity or an earlier AI call) is left exactly as it is: no second write and no overwritten reason.

The customer did something (customerActive: true, or awaitingCustomerReply: false — "the customer replied"): restart the Website/Chatbot inactivity clock from now. Recorded only for a live Website/Chatbot conversation whose ticket is still open and not human-managed; otherwise it is a no-op. A repeat inside the same instant changes nothing.

The chatbot inactivity timer's only writer on the request path.
Only an active chatbot exchange can be waiting. A timer is never started — and a running one is cancelled — when human follow-up is outstanding or being requested in this same update (requested handoff, bot connection failure, takeover), when a person already owns the ticket, or when the ticket or conversation is over. Those are exactly the cases the closing job re-checks again at fire time; doing it here as well keeps the persisted state honest rather than relying on the job alone.
Idempotent. awaitingCustomerReply: true while a timer is running changes nothing (), so a redelivered webhook cannot restart it. Returns a note only when a requested timer was deliberately not started.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.IdentityAndAccess.Services.AssignableUserAppService
member.summary: The cross-department assignee directory: every active employee who is a member of at least one active department, with their roles and ALL their department memberships (primary first). Backs GET /api/users/assignable, which a CS Manager reads when the ticket's current department holds nobody suitable and the ticket must be transferred to the assignee's department and assigned in one step.

remarks.para: One row per employee, however many departments they belong to — the UI chooses the (employee, department) pair, and the assignment rule ("the assignee belongs to the ticket's resulting department") is enforced by TicketAssignmentAppService, never by this listing.
This is a directory, not an authorization decision: it lists who exists. Whether the caller may assign at all is the endpoint's policy and the assignment service's role gate.

member.summary: Stateless JWT with no revocation list is used at MVP (no refresh-token or token-revocation mechanism is specified in the approved API contract, and none is invented here). Logout is a client-side token discard; this method exists as the seam for the audit entry the contract describes, once the Audit module (S-05, out of scope for this increment) exists.

member.name: M:TigerCS.Application.Modules.IdentityAndAccess.Services.AuthenticationAppService.ChangePasswordAsync(System.Guid,TigerCS.Application.Modules.IdentityAndAccess.Dto.ChangePasswordRequestDto,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Changes the caller's own password. Identity verifies the current password and applies the password policy; a wrong current password is reported as exactly that and nothing more. On success Identity rotates the security stamp, which — because every token carries the stamp it was issued under — invalidates every session the user had, including the one that made this call: the client must sign in again. Audited as ChangeOwnPassword without any secret.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Abstractions.ICustomerEmailSender
member.summary:
The customer-facing email boundary — what a notification handler calls to get one rendered customer email delivered.
Sits one level above (the raw provider adapter). This port owns the customer-notification rules that every notification type shares and no provider should have to know: the EmailNotifications:Enabled switch, recipient validation, turning a provider exception into a classified result, and the outcome log line. A handler therefore never has to guard those itself, and adding a new notification type is a template plus a handler — not another copy of the safety rules.
Never throws for a delivery problem and never decides who the recipient is: the address arrives already resolved from trusted ticket data (CustomerContactResolver), and an address that is missing or malformed is reported as , never guessed or defaulted.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Abstractions.IEmailSender
member.summary:
The email-provider boundary — Module-Design.md's IEmailGateway "external adapter contract" for the Notifications module, named IEmailSender to say what it does rather than what layer it lives in.
Deliberately the narrowest possible surface. One operation, a value-typed message in, a classified result out. No provider concept (SMTP host, Graph client, API key, tenant) crosses it, so provider configuration cannot leak into business logic and swapping Office 365 for an SMTP relay touches one adapter and nothing else. The same shape ICrmGateway already uses.
Returns a classified result rather than throwing. Whether a failure is worth retrying is provider knowledge — a 4xx "no such mailbox" and a 5xx "greylisted, try later" are not the same event, and the dispatcher must not have to guess by inspecting exception types it does not own. An adapter that throws anyway is still handled (the dispatcher treats an unclassified exception as transient, the safer direction), but classifying is the contract.

member.summary:
Persists a dispatch claim, reporting whether this caller won it.
Separate from because losing the claim race is a routine, expected outcome — two workers polling the same batch — not an exception the dispatcher should have to catch per message. false means another worker already owns the message.

member.name: M:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Abstractions.INotificationsUnitOfWork.DiscardPendingChangesAsync(System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary:
Abandons everything staged but not yet committed, returning the unit of work to a clean state.
The dispatcher processes a batch through one unit of work, so a message whose handler threw — or whose outcome failed to save — must not leave half-written entities behind for the next message's commit to pick up and persist. Without this, one poisoned message could corrupt the message after it.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Abstractions.IOutboxEventHandler
member.summary:
One consumer of one Outbox EventType. The dispatcher owns claiming, retry accounting and dead-lettering; a handler owns only "what this event means".
Every handler must be idempotent (ADR-0013's own consequence: "every consumer of an Outbox message must itself be idempotent"). Delivery is at-least-once — a process that dies between a successful send and its commit will re-run this handler — so a handler that cannot recognise already-done work will duplicate a customer-visible effect.

member.summary:
The Application layer's view of the CustomerNotifications section — one Boolean switch.
IsTestMode = true: every customer email goes to TestEmail and every customer SMS to TestPhone; the customer's own contact details are never used. IsTestMode = false: messages go to their intended recipients.
Fails safe. Only an explicit false turns test mode off; a missing, blank or unrecognised value means test mode. In test mode a missing or invalid recipient suppresses that delivery — there is no fallback to the customer.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Dto.TicketCreatedEventPayload
member.summary:
The TicketCreated Outbox payload (MVP-API-Contracts.md §3.1/§2.6).
Identifiers only, deliberately. No requester name, no contact channel, no request summary. An Outbox row is long-lived and operator-visible, and Security-Architecture.md §11 requires customer contact details be masked or omitted from operational output — so the handler re-reads whatever it needs from the database at dispatch time instead. The cost is one extra read per dispatch; the benefit is that no customer data is duplicated into an infrastructure table at all.
is part of ADR-0014's idempotency key (TicketId + EventType + EventVersion) and is carried in the payload too so a consumer reading an old row can tell which shape it is looking at.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.NotificationAuditActions
member.summary:
The AuditEntries.Action values this module writes (ADR-0018 §2 — the generic table, since a notification delivery is not a change to one of the five ticket-state dimensions and so does not belong in TicketStatusHistory).
Together these five make FR-NOT-05's "all notification sends/failures are logged, correlation-tracked" a property of the audit trail rather than of log retention: every one carries the Outbox message's own correlation ID, so a delivery can be traced end-to-end across the audit trail, the Outbox and structured logs from one identifier (ADR-0014).
No entry ever carries a message body, address or secret. BeforeValue/AfterValue hold status transitions, attempt counts and identifiers only. Security-Architecture.md §11's masking rule is written for logs; an audit row is longer-lived and more widely readable, so it gets the stricter treatment — not the looser one.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.OutboxDispatchPolicy
member.summary: The retry, dead-letter and batching policy the dispatcher applies (ADR-0013). A plain value, not an IOptions<T>: the Application project deliberately depends on nothing but the Domain, and configuration binding belongs to the composition root. Infrastructure's OutboxDispatchOptions binds the configuration section and projects it into this.
member.param:
Attempts before a message dead-letters.
An assumption carried over, not a new decision. No merged document states a threshold for the general Outbox. The only approved number anywhere is MVP-API-Contracts.md §6.1's [ASSUMPTION] 5 failed processing attempts for Genesys events, and MVP-Design-Review-Checklist.md §12 records that the retry/dead-letter policy is "the same mechanism referenced for both Genesys events and general notifications" — so one threshold across both consumers is what that checklist item asks for.

Base unit of the exponential backoff (). At 30 seconds, retries become eligible 30s / 90s / 210s / 450s after the event — about seven minutes of patience before dead-lettering, enough to absorb a brief provider blip without leaving a customer waiting hours for an acknowledgement. No merged document specifies a curve; this is a tuning value, which is why it is configurable rather than fixed.
Messages examined per pass, so a backlog drains steadily instead of monopolising a worker.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Services.CustomerContactResolver
member.summary:
Resolves the customer a ticket's notifications go to — name and email — from the ticket's own persisted data and nothing else.
Sources, in order of trust. No column on Tickets holds a customer email, and this increment deliberately adds none: two reliable fields already exist and are consulted in this order —
— the CRM contact verified at ticket creation (ADR-0007's immutable snapshot). It is an untyped "phone or email" value, so it counts only when it is unambiguously an email address.
— the email Genesys supplied with the inquiry, captured on the originating interaction (falling back to the most recent interaction that carries one).
Never guesses. A ticket with neither yields = ; a value that exists but is not a usable address yields . There is no fallback mailbox, and the reason never echoes the value itself.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Services.CustomerDeliveryGuardEmailSender
member.summary:
The final delivery boundary for email: wraps the provider adapter so that CustomerNotifications:IsTestMode is applied to every caller — ticket notifications, OTP codes, document copies, Collections reminders, anything added later — including background jobs. No code path reaches the provider with a customer-facing message except through this class.
(staff, administrators): always passes untouched.
(the default, so a caller that forgets to classify is guarded): production sends as addressed; test mode replaces the recipient with TestEmail (and marks the subject [TEST]), or — when TestEmail is missing or invalid — skips the message and logs a warning. The customer's address is never used.
A skipped message is reported as — terminal, never retried, never an error.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Services.CustomerEmailSender
member.summary:
The default : applies the shared customer-notification rules, then delegates the actual delivery to whichever adapter is configured.
What is logged. Exactly one line per call: notification type, ticket number, masked recipient, outcome, reason, correlation ID. Never the subject or body (customer content), never the full address, and — structurally — never a credential: this class has no access to any.
What is never thrown. A provider that throws is turned into a transient result carrying only the exception's type name. The caller — an Outbox handler running in a background job — can therefore never take a ticket operation down, and a provider message that might echo a server banner or an address never reaches a persisted error column.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Services.CustomerTicketEmailHandler
member.summary:
The shared shape of every customer-facing ticket email consumed from the Outbox: load the ticket, find-or-create the delivery row, resolve the customer, render, send through , record the outcome. Subclasses contribute only what differs — the event type, the notification type, the template, and any extra guard or ticket write-back.
Idempotent, as ADR-0013 requires of every Outbox consumer. The dispatcher delivers at least once, so a handler can run twice for one event. The Notifications row is found rather than recreated and a terminal one (Sent, Skipped, DeadLettered) is never acted on again; a unique index on (OutboxMessageId, NotificationType) turns a genuine race into a constraint violation rather than two rows. Subclasses may add a domain guard via .
Skipping is a first-class, successful outcome. Disabled notifications, a ticket with no usable email, or an event too old to still be worth sending all end as with a audit entry naming the reason, and the Outbox message is Processed. They are expected, countable, and never inflate the dead-letter alerts.
Never sends inside a transaction and never saves. The dispatcher commits once per message after this returns.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Services.OutboxDispatcher
member.summary:
ADR-0013's dispatcher, driven by ADR-0015's recurring Hangfire job. Reads pending OutboxMessages and hands each to the handler registered for its EventType.
Owns reliability; handlers own meaning. Claiming, attempt accounting, backoff, dead-lettering and the audit trail live here, once, for every event type — which is exactly ADR-0013's stated advantage over a bespoke reliability mechanism per integration.
Two commits per message, and the provider call sits between them. The claim commits first so no second worker can take the same message; then the handler runs, including its network call, with no transaction held; then the outcome commits. Sending inside a transaction would pin database locks for the provider's latency.
Nothing is ever discarded. A message either becomes Processed, stays Pending for another attempt, or becomes DeadLettered and is kept for review (FR-NOT-05). There is no branch that deletes a row or silently swallows a failure — an unexpected exception is caught only so one bad message cannot stall the batch, and it is recorded on the message as a failed attempt like any other.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Services.TicketAcknowledgementHandler
member.summary:
FR-NOT-01 / backlog S-18 — the automated "we have received your request" email, consumed from the TicketCreated Outbox event.
This path never satisfies the First Response SLA. FR-SLA-05 and ISSUE-019 exist because an acknowledgement fires within seconds of creation and would otherwise "satisfy" every first-response target automatically. A successful send writes exactly one ticket field, AcknowledgementSentAtUtc, via ; nothing here references any service that could record a first response.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Templates.CustomerEmailTemplates
member.summary:
The customer-facing email templates — one method per notification, all rendered through one shared Tiger Properties layout so header, footer and signature can never drift between notification types.
Layout. A table-based, inline-CSS design that renders in Outlook (a 650px ghost table for Word-engine clients, max-width for the rest), with the Tiger Properties branding: a white page with a thin gold (#C1A562) outer border, the original logo over a thin light-grey divider, gold rating stars, and a white footer with the team, phone, website and customer-service mailbox. No gradients, shadows or coloured backgrounds. English and Arabic are both supported; Arabic renders right-to-left. There is no script, form or other interactive element — the only interaction is a link.
Every dynamic value is HTML-encoded on its way into the HTML body (), and the plain-text body is built from the same values without markup. Names, ticket numbers, request-type names and resolution notes are all customer- or agent-supplied text and are treated as untrusted. Links are rendered only when they are absolute http(s) URLs.
Nothing internal is rendered. Templates receive only the fields listed on : no database or employee identifiers, no queue or workflow identifiers, no SLA state, no internal notes. Adding a field here is a deliberate, reviewable act.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Reporting.Services.TeamPerformanceAppService
member.summary:
The CS Manager's Team Performance report: one row per eligible agent with four counts, and the records behind any one count.
Who is on the report. Every ACTIVE employee holding one of in Identity — today exactly the "CS Agent" role. There is no separate "Call Center Agent" role: per docs/Genesys/Genesys-Cloud-Configuration.md §4, call-centre agents are CS Agents who belong to the Call Center department (code ). The report therefore derives an agent type per employee from department membership rather than from a role, and shows one row per employee however many roles or departments they hold. Employees with no activity in the period are included with zeros.
Period. UTC calendar days, inclusive, defaulting to the last 30 days exactly as the Dashboard does (). Currently Assigned is the one current-state figure and ignores the period.
Read-only: nothing here changes state, so no audit entry is written. Authorization (CS Manager / General Manager / Chairman-CEO, plus the System Administrator override) is the Api's policy, not decided here.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Abstractions.IIdempotencyRecordStore
member.summary:
ADR-0014's idempotency mechanism, over IdempotencyRecords (MVP-Data-Dictionary.md §2.23).
Reserving a key is a claim, not a query: the caller proceeds only if the claim succeeded. That is what lets SLA-Architecture.md §13's scheduled job and §14's safety sweep both target the same due event without the second one duplicating its effects.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Abstractions.SlaBreachIdempotencyKey
member.summary:
Builds the breach-check idempotency key of SLA-Architecture.md §15 — TicketId + CheckType + DueTimestamp.
The due timestamp is part of the key deliberately: if a later increment recomputes a deadline (backlog S-14's priority upgrade moves both due dates), the new deadline is a genuinely different due event and must be checkable, while re-checking the old one stays suppressed. Round- tripped through "O" so the key text is culture-invariant and exact to the tick.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Abstractions.ISlaDeadlineScheduler
member.summary:
ADR-0015 / SLA-Architecture.md §13 — the primary breach-detection mechanism: a scheduled (delayed) background job enqueued per due timestamp at the moment it is computed, so the check fires at the exact due moment rather than waiting for a poll.
Abstracted here so the application layer never references Hangfire directly (Module-Design.md's dependency rules) and so the correctness of breach detection can be tested without a scheduler at all — the work a fired job performs lives in SlaBreachDetectionAppService, which is a plain service with no scheduling concern of its own.
Scheduling is an optimisation, never the guarantee. SLA-Architecture.md §14's recurring sweep independently re-scans due deadlines, so a job lost to a deploy or restart — or never enqueued at all, which is what the no-op implementation does — still results in the breach being detected. Both paths converge on the same idempotency key (§15), so whichever runs second changes nothing.

Critical / High / Medium / Low, or null when the ticket has no priority.

The Resolution target of the applied policy, in minutes.
"24/7" or "Business hours".
Share of the target after which the ticket counts as at risk.
The business calendar in force (working hours, zone, working days, holidays) — only when the basis is business hours.
When the current period's clock started (the period start), or null when none.
Why the current period exists: InitialCreation, Upgrade, Downgrade or Reopen.
Plain-language reason there is no running SLA, or null when there is one.
What counts as the first human response — and what does not.
How pausing works in this release.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Services.FirstHumanResponseRecorder
member.summary:
The one place Ticket.FirstHumanResponseAtUtc is satisfied, and everything that must happen with it: the lifecycle history row, the audit entry, and the breach finalization that turns a late first response into a recorded breach (and its automatic Level 2 escalation).
Why this exists rather than a second mechanism. First Response is reached two ways: a person recording it through POST /api/tickets/{id}/sla/first-response (, which owns the authorization and optimistic-concurrency half), and the system observing it when the first genuinely human message of a conversation is stored (GenesysConversationEndAppService). Those are different callers with different permission stories, but the consequence is identical, and ISSUE-019's whole point is that this measurement must be written in exactly one way. Both therefore call this.
What is deliberately NOT here. No authorization — the API path gates itself and the system path has no user to gate. No transaction and no SaveChangesAsync — this enlists in the caller's unit of work, the same contract SlaDueDateService and TicketAutoAssignmentService follow, so the response and whatever prompted it commit together or not at all. No RowVersion handling: the caller decides whether a stale token is a conflict.
An AI or automated reply can never reach this. The automated acknowledgement has its own column (Ticket.AcknowledgementSentAtUtc), and the transcript path calls this only for lines — never . FR-SLA-05 / ISSUE-019 exist precisely because a machine responding instantly would otherwise satisfy every first-response target and make the KPI meaningless.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Services.PriorityDowngradeAppService
member.summary:
The priority-downgrade approval workflow (ISSUE-023 Option B; MVP-API-Contracts.md section 5.6; MVP-ERD.md section 2.27).
A downgrade never takes effect on request. Requesting creates a Pending and nothing else: the ticket's priority and its current SLA period are untouched while it waits.
Who decides. A Department Head holding membership of the ticket's current department, or a CS Manager / General Manager (the "Dept Head and above" tier, cross-department), or a System Administrator via ADR-0024's central override. The decider is always the authenticated caller, never a request field. The requester can never decide their own request (even under the override): the contract is silent on self-approval, so the safe separation-of-duties answer is applied and listed as an open decision. Chairman/CEO is not in the set: the contract's "above" is read as the existing CS Manager / GM tiers.
Approval is one transaction. Re-validate (Pending, not expired, ticket not final, priority unchanged since the request), then in a single unit of work: the request becomes Approved, the ticket's priority changes, the current SLA period ends and a Downgrade period opens, and the audit rows are staged. Anything fallible (the new policy lookup) runs before any state changes; a failed save rolls everything back.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Services.SlaBreachDetectionAppService
member.summary:
The entry point both background-job paths of ADR-0015 call (backlog S-10).
— SLA-Architecture.md §13's primary mechanism: one scheduled (delayed) job per due timestamp, enqueued when the timestamp is computed and firing at the due moment.
— §14's backstop only: a recurring re-scan that exists solely to catch a scheduled job lost to a deploy or restart. It is never the primary detection path.
Neither path depends on a browser, a SignalR client, or any connected user. Detection is server-side background work against stored due timestamps (FR-SLA-04: the columns "exist and are queryable independent of any background job"; ADR-0016 restricts SignalR to state-change notification and explicitly not to countdown or detection).
Each ticket is its own transaction. A sweep covering many tickets must not lose the work already done for earlier ones because a later one failed, and a per-ticket commit keeps the idempotency claim and the effects it guards atomic.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Services.SlaBreachProcessor
member.summary:
The single place a breach is decided and recorded (backlog S-10/S-11, FR-SLA-01–04, FR-ESC-02).
Three callers, one code path. SLA-Architecture.md §13's scheduled job, §14's safety sweep, and the two achievement events (recording the First Human Response, and resolving the ticket) all arrive here. That is what makes the idempotency guarantee real rather than per-caller: every path composes the same TicketId + CheckType + DueTimestamp key (§15/ADR-0014), so whichever arrives second writes nothing at all — no second breach flag, no second escalation row, no second audit entry.
Boundary semantics. A deadline not yet satisfied is breached once now >= due — the scheduled job fires at the due moment (§13), so an exclusive comparison would mean it could never fire. A deadline that was satisfied is breached only if the satisfying event landed strictly after the due moment, so satisfying it exactly on the deadline is on time. The two rules agree at the boundary instant.
Participates in the caller's transaction — nothing here calls SaveChanges. The breach flag, the escalation row, the history rows and the audit entries must all commit together or not at all.

member.summary:
FR-ESC-02 / backlog S-11 — "a breach automatically raises a Level 2 TicketEscalations row".
Exactly one per ticket, which is backlog S-11's own stated test requirement ("exactly one Level 2 escalation, not a repeating one on every subsequent check"). ADR-0011 models the level as a state rather than a counter, so a second breach on the other clock re-escalating a ticket already sitting with the Department Head would be a duplicate, not new information. The filtered unique index on TicketEscalations is the concurrent-race backstop behind this check.
The ticket's own level only rises. If a CS Manager has already taken the ticket to Level 3 or 4, the automatic escalation is still recorded — the breach genuinely occurred and the recipient matrix still applies — but the ticket is not pulled back down to Level 2.
TicketStatus is never touched. Escalation is an independent dimension (ADR-0008/ADR-0011): an escalated ticket stays exactly as Open, InProgress or Resolved as it already was.

Opens a ticket's initial SLA period: computes both due timestamps from the seeded policy and calendar, persists them as the ticket's current , audits the computation, and schedules the two deadline checks (backlog S-08/S-09, FR-SLA-01–04).

member.name: M:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Services.SlaDueDateService.StartReopenResolutionCycleAsync(TigerCS.Domain.Modules.Ticketing.Ticket,System.DateTime,System.Nullable{System.Guid},System.Guid,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary:
The approved Reopen rule's SLA behaviour: end the ticket's current SLA period at the reopen moment and open a successor whose Resolution clock starts there, computed from the same policy and calendar as any other period — never a hard-coded duration.
First Response is never restarted. Its due timestamp and breach flag are carried across verbatim (see ), and no First Response deadline check is scheduled: that clock's result was settled on the original cycle and reopening must not re-open, re-arm or re-flag it.
This is what stops a reopened ticket breaching instantly. The old period's long-past ResolutionDueAtUtc leaves the sweep's candidate set the moment that period is ended (the sweep reads current periods only), and the successor carries a deadline in the future — so the reopened ticket is neither auto-breached nor auto-escalated on the strength of a deadline that belonged to work already delivered. The old row keeps its own flags untouched, so the original cycle stays honestly reportable (ISSUE-023).
Participates in the caller's transaction, like . Returns null — writing nothing — when the ticket has no current period at all (a provisional ticket still awaiting reconciliation, or an unclassified one): reopening such a ticket must not invent an SLA clock it never had.
member.param: The ticket being reopened. Its PriorityId selects the policy.
The reopen moment — where the old period ends and the new Resolution clock starts.
The reopening agent, for the audit entry.
Shared with the reopen's other rows so one action reads as one event.
Cancels the operation.
member.returns: The newly opened cycle, or null when the ticket has no SLA period to succeed.

member.summary:
Re-applies the governing policy to the ticket's running period after a request type was classified onto it (a Genesys ticket opens on the Normal priority policy and learns its request type later).
Never restarts, shortens-by-erasure or forgives. Due times are recomputed from the period's original start, so elapsed time stays elapsed; the period row, its start and its breach flags are kept. A deadline is left exactly as it is when it is already breached, when First Response has already been satisfied by a human, or (Resolution) when the period has pause history — a recomputed deadline would drop the time already added by the pause. Nothing is written when the result would not differ.
Participates in the caller's transaction. Returns when the ticket has no running period to adjust.

member.summary:
The SLA side of an approved priority downgrade (ISSUE-023 Option B; SLA-Architecture.md section 7): end the current period at the approval moment and open a successor under the new priority's policy.
Nothing recorded is removed. The ended period keeps its breach flags and its dates, so management reporting shows both the original and the changed period. First Response is carried verbatim (never restarted or loosened, as for a reopen). The Resolution deadline is recomputed from the approval moment under the new policy, and is never earlier than the deadline already in effect, so a downgrade can only ever relax the future deadline and never create a tighter one.
Everything fallible (the policy lookup) runs before any state is touched, so a failure leaves the period unended. Participates in the caller's transaction. Returns null, writing nothing, when the ticket has no current period (provisional or unclassified): the SLA will be opened later from the ticket's then-current priority.

member.summary:
SLA pause/resume (ISSUE-018, SLA-Architecture.md §6/§8) — the one writer of .
Driven by the ticket's status, never by a separate command. A lifecycle service mutates and then calls ; this service compares the status with the ticket's open pause and does whatever is needed: open one, close one, or nothing. That makes every entry point idempotent by construction — a repeated Pending Customer entry finds the open pause and writes nothing, a duplicate resume finds none and writes nothing — and means the same code handles the ordinary status change, Resolve, Close and the system inactivity closure.
What pauses. Only the Resolution clock, only while the ticket is Pending Customer (or legacy Pending Third Party), never a Critical period, and not when the request type's explicit PausesOnPendingCustomer is false (). First Response never pauses. A deadline already missed is recorded as a breach before any pause opens, and a period that has already breached Resolution does not pause (the breach is permanent; extending its deadline would rewrite history).
On resume the deadline moves, nothing else does. See . Elapsed time, breach flags and period history are untouched; the pause row keeps the deadline before and after. The new deadline is handed to ; the job scheduled for the old one is harmless — it fires, finds the extended deadline in the future, and records nothing.
Participates in the caller's transaction — nothing here calls SaveChanges.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Services.SlaRoleSets
member.summary:
Per-action role sets for SLA and escalation authorization, mirroring TicketRoleSets's design exactly: each action gets its own set, stating what the permission matrix grants, and every consumer routes its decision through AuthorizationGate.
System Administrator is deliberately absent from every set below, and is authorized anyway. ADR-0024's central override is applied by the gate before any set here is consulted, and by SystemAdministratorOverrideHandler for the policy layer. Naming the role in these lists is exactly the per-call-site duplication that correction's requirement 4 rules out — and it would erase the distinction these sets exist to record: what the permission matrix grants, as against what the override grants on top of it.

member.name: F:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Services.SlaRoleSets.RecordFirstResponse
member.summary: Record the First Human Response (MVP-API-Contracts.md §5.2, "Agent and above") — the ticket's current owner, or a supervisory role. Ownership is checked separately against the ticket itself, exactly as TicketLifecycleAppService does for a status change; this set is the cross-department authority that stands in for it.

member.name: F:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Services.SlaRoleSets.ManualEscalate
member.summary: Raise a manual escalation with ManualFlag (MVP-API-Contracts.md §5.7, "Agent and above"). Includes the department-side roles because FR-ESC-01's flag-for-escalation is the action a working agent takes when they cannot resolve a ticket themselves (Solution-Analysis.md §7.6, Level 1), and a Department Employee working the ticket is exactly that actor. Department-scoped callers are additionally checked against the ticket's own department.

member.name: F:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Services.SlaRoleSets.ManualLevel4Escalate
member.summary: Level 4 (Chairman/CEO) escalation: CS Manager or GM only (MVP-ERD.md §2.17 — "`TriggerType = ManualLevel4` rows may only be inserted by a CS Manager or GM actor"; MVP-API-Contracts.md §5.7's `403` validation rule). Deliberately narrower than , and never widened by a level check alone — see TicketEscalationAppService.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Services.TicketEscalationAppService
member.summary:
Manual escalation (MVP-API-Contracts.md §5.7, FR-ESC-01, backlog S-11).
Escalation is a dimension, not a status. Nothing here reads or writes TicketStatus, ResolutionOutcome or DuplicateOfTicketId: a ticket escalated to any level stays exactly as Open or InProgress as it was, which is the whole reason ADR-0008 split the five dimensions apart in the first place ("a ticket may remain In Progress while escalated" cannot be expressed in a single-status model).
Level 4 is manual-only and doubly gated. MVP-ERD.md §2.17 restricts ManualLevel4 rows to a CS Manager or GM actor, and MVP-API-Contracts.md §5.7 answers a violation with 403. Because the contract carries Level and TriggerType as two independent client-supplied fields, the role gate alone is not sufficient: a CS Agent could otherwise send Level = 4 with TriggerType = ManualFlag and reach Level 4 without ever meeting the gate. The pairing is therefore rejected as well — closing a bypass of the approved rule, not adding a new one.

Manual escalation (MVP-API-Contracts.md §5.7, FR-ESC-01, backlog S-11).
Escalation is a dimension, not a status. Nothing here reads or writes TicketStatus, ResolutionOutcome or DuplicateOfTicketId: a ticket escalated to any level stays exactly as Open or InProgress as it was, which is the whole reason ADR-0008 split the five dimensions apart in the first place ("a ticket may remain In Progress while escalated" cannot be expressed in a single-status model).
Level 4 is manual-only and doubly gated. MVP-ERD.md §2.17 restricts ManualLevel4 rows to a CS Manager or GM actor, and MVP-API-Contracts.md §5.7 answers a violation with 403. Because the contract carries Level and TriggerType as two independent client-supplied fields, the role gate alone is not sufficient: a CS Agent could otherwise send Level = 4 with TriggerType = ManualFlag and reach Level 4 without ever meeting the gate. The pairing is therefore rejected as well — closing a bypass of the approved rule, not adding a new one.

MVP-API-Contracts.md §5.7's two-tier rule: "Agent and above for ManualFlag; CS Manager or GM only for ManualLevel4". Both tiers are permission rules, so both run through the gate and pick up the ADR-0024 override without naming the role.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Abstractions.ApprovalApproverScope
member.summary:
Everything a repository needs to decide, SQL-side, which Pending approvals one caller is authorized to action — the set-based twin of TicketApprovalAppService.IsAuthorizedApproverAsync's per-record rule, resolved once per request from the caller's own roles and department memberships (never client-supplied):
Employee target: the target employee is the caller.
Role target: the caller holds the target role.
Department target: the caller is a member of the target department AND holds the requirement's narrowing role when one is named, otherwise one of TicketApprovalAppService.DepartmentTargetDefaultApproverRoles.
: the ADR-0024 applies, so every Pending approval is actionable — exactly as AuthorizationGate would answer per record.
Used by the Dashboard's Pending Approval KPI and the ticket queue's pendingApproval drill-down filter, so the number and the list always agree.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Abstractions.DashboardOverviewQuery
member.summary:
The Operational Dashboard's one read (Dashboard Phase 1). Follows the exact scoping discipline of : is resolved server-side by the application service from the caller's roles/department membership, already intersected with any requested department filter — it is never client-supplied and a filter can only narrow it, never widen it. Null means no department restriction (cross-department view role); an empty set means "nothing visible" and every count comes back zero.
Two time contexts, deliberately distinct. KPIs, Open Backlog Ageing and the Recent/Critical list are current-state: they cover every active ticket in scope regardless of when it was created, so an old open ticket is never hidden by a recent date range. The volume breakdowns (channel, request type, department, status, priority) are historical: tickets created within [, ). The dimension filters (department, agent, channel, request type, status, priority) apply to both.
The four closure KPIs (Reviewed, Not Reviewed, Closed by AI, Closed by Agent) are the exception to "KPIs are current-state": they count Closed tickets, which are by definition not part of the active backlog, so they follow the date range applied to the ticket's latest closure date ([, )) and the same dimension filters — except the status filter: they always represent Closed tickets, whatever status the Dashboard has selected.
member.param: Null = no restriction; otherwise the departments the counts may cover.
For the My Tickets count.
For the Pending Approval count — approvals the caller is authorized to action.
Agent filter: tickets currently owned by this employee.
Channel filter: the ticket's originating interaction channel.
Request type filter.
Status filter.
Priority filter.
Inclusive start of the volume date range.
Exclusive end of the volume date range.
The evaluation instant — passed in so the query is deterministic under test.
Start of "today" (UTC calendar day) for Due Today.
How far ahead of a pending SLA deadline ranks as "due soon" in the Recent/Critical list.
Maximum Recent/Critical rows.
Set only for a restricted CS Agent: every count and list is then limited to tickets assigned to, or handled on Genesys by, that employee (plus , empty for a CS Agent). See TicketQuery.

Department filter applied on top of the scope (the current department). Used when the scope is not itself a department set, i.e. for a restricted CS Agent; for everyone else the requested department is already folded into .

Which reviews count as customer feedback for the Reviewed / Not Reviewed KPIs: Test-mode reviews while customer notifications run in test mode (UAT), real reviews otherwise. Production satisfaction statistics are unaffected.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Abstractions.CustomerHistoryQuery
member.summary: Customer History (Customer → Previous Ticket History, this increment). Exactly one of / is ever meaningful — the CRM-verified identity (CrmBuyerCustomerId) and the phone-snapshot fallback identity are never combined into one query (see CustomerHistoryAppService's remarks for why: a phone number is not a trusted unique customer identity, so it must never widen a verified customer's own history). is the fallback path's pre-resolved set — the ticket ids linked from an IntakeRecord recorded against the same phone number (IIntakeRecordRepository.ListLinkedTicketIdsByPhoneNumberAsync) — kept out of this repository so it never needs to join across the IntakeRecord aggregate itself.
member.remarks:
The Customer Workspace phase adds a third identity: + — the persisted external verification identity a PACT/Tasleeh ticket carries (Ticket.CustomerVerificationSource/Ticket.ExternalCustomerId). Exactly one of the three identities is ever set per query; the external pair always travels together, and external history is never matched by display name or phone number — two customers sharing a phone must never share a history.
Duplicate-ticket awareness (Phase E) adds two refinements, both applied inside this same single query — never a per-row follow-up: narrows the identity's history to one unit (exact match on the ticket's CRM Buyer or manual unit-number snapshot — deterministic, no fuzzy matching), and sorts currently-active tickets ahead of Resolved/Closed ones (newest first within each group), so the most actionable related tickets surface within the limit.

member.name: M:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Abstractions.ITicketStatusHistoryRepository.GetLatestTransitionIntoAsync(System.Int64,TigerCS.Domain.Modules.Ticketing.TicketStatusDimension,System.Byte,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary:
The most recent transition of INTO for one ticket, or null when it never happened.
Exists because the approved Reopen rule measures its window from the moment a ticket was closed, and a Closed ticket carries no closure timestamp column of its own. Rather than inventing one — or substituting the resolution timestamp, which is a different moment — the window reads the lifecycle history CloseAsync has always written. "Most recent" matters: a ticket closed, reopened and closed again is measured from its latest closure, never its first.

One ticket's full lifecycle history, oldest first. Append-only and never filtered — this is the record, not a summary of it.
The read half of ADR-0018's store, added so Ticket Details can finally show what the table has always held: until now nothing exposed it, so the Activity feed could show only notes and escalations, and the reopen reason agents were required to type was written and never seen. Serving the existing rows was the alternative to inventing a second activity store beside them.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Abstractions.TicketClosureCategory
member.summary:
The four Dashboard closure KPIs, which are also the ticket queue's closureCategory filter — so a card and its drill-down list are computed by one predicate. Every category covers currently Closed tickets only, counted once per ticket.
Reviewed / NotReviewed split the closed tickets by whether the customer submitted a satisfaction review (TicketReviews) for the ticket's current cycle (ReopenCycle = Ticket.ReopenCount). Reviews flagged IsTest (Test-mode links) are not customer feedback and are ignored, exactly as production satisfaction reporting ignores them. An invitation without a submission is not a review.
ClosedByAi / ClosedByAgent are decided by the ticket's most recent closing audit entry (see ): AutoCloseByAi is the Genesys AI closure, Close is a person closing the ticket. Every other closure — chatbot inactivity, document delivery — is neither, and a reopened ticket is judged by how it was closed the last time.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Abstractions.TicketConcurrentlyModifiedException
member.summary: Thrown when a lost optimistic-concurrency race is detected on Tickets.RowVersion — another request modified the same ticket (assignment, transfer, status change, resolve, close, or reconciliation) between this request's read and its write. The caller should surface a `409`/`412` and let the client retry against the ticket's current state (its own `If-Match` header pattern, mirroring MVP-API-Contracts.md's other mutating ticket endpoints).

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Abstractions.VerificationSessionConcurrentlyConsumedException
member.summary: Thrown by when persisting a VerificationSession consumption loses an optimistic-concurrency race — two concurrent ticket-creation requests both read the same Confirmed session before either committed, both passed the in-memory Consume() check, and only one write can win (MVP-ERD.md §2.24's single-use invariant, enforced here at the database level via a concurrency token on VerificationSessions.Status — see TigerCsDbContext's supplemental configuration). The losing caller's session is, by the time this is thrown, genuinely already consumed by the winner — translated by TicketCreationAppService to the same VerificationSessionAlreadyConsumed outcome a sequential replay would get, not a raw 500.

member.name: F:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Dto.AgentHandoffOutcome.AlreadyClaimed
member.summary: Another agent already holds this work. Deliberately distinct from : the claim is exclusive, and answering a second agent with success — carrying the first agent's assignee — is how two people end up calling the same customer.

member.name: F:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Dto.AgentHandoffOutcome.ConcurrencyConflict
F:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Dto.AgentHandoffOutcome.AgentNotInTicketDepartment
member.summary:
The accepting employee is not an active member of the ticket's current department, so accepting would have to assign the ticket to a non-member — which MVP-API-Contracts.md §3.5 forbids and TicketAssignmentAppService.AssignAsync already refuses as EmployeeNotInDepartment.
Checked before anything is claimed. Accepting is one operation: claim the work, own the ticket, start it. A caller who cannot complete all three must change nothing, or the system ends up in the state this outcome exists to prevent — handoff InProgress while the ticket sits Open and unowned, which reads as "someone is on it" to the queue and "nobody owns this" to the ticket.
Not an authorization failure, and deliberately distinct from : the caller may well be entitled to see and act on this department's work (the CS layer is cross-department for visibility). What they cannot do is become the ticket's owner. The route to handling it is the existing Department Transfer, after which a member of the new current department accepts.
The ADR-0024 override does not reach this. The override answers "may this caller act at all"; department membership of the assignee is a domain invariant about the ticket's data, not a permission. A System Administrator may therefore see and administer work anywhere and still not assign a ticket to themselves in a department they do not belong to.

member.name: F:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Ticketing.Dto.AgentHandoffOutcome.TicketClosed
member.summary: The ticket behind this work is Closed, so it can take neither an owner nor a status change (closed-ticket immutability). Refused rather than claiming the work and leaving it attached to a ticket nothing can move — stand the work down instead.
